acv.quote: Ninety-five K ACV, on a two-year term.

data.reason: The CFO decided from a one-page comparison of our rate against the bank's sharpened rate, and nothing from us showed what Fernbrook's failed orders were costing, so he saw 'the same thing' for more money. Sam blames price, but the evidence points to a missing value case in the customer's own numbers. He also admits IT's worry about moving before spring meant it was 'maybe not only the rate.'

trigger.finding: Lucy came inbound because online orders were failing at checkout, worst on large orders, and the processor couldn't tell her why. Our messaging could aim at the moment a retailer sees big-ticket orders failing on their own dashboard with no explanation from their processor.
trigger.quote: She said about one in twelve online orders was failing at the payment step, and it was worse on the big baskets.

decider.finding: The CFO, Martin, made the call, and Sam knows it only because Lucy told him. Martin was not our champion, and Sam never met him because Martin doesn't take vendor meetings. Lucy, who had called approval a formality, carried our case into a meeting we weren't in.
decider.quote: Martin said no. Lucy told me. I never met him.

competitor.finding: Per Lucy, the incumbent bank responded with only a better rate and no new product. After that her questions moved from why big orders fail to whether we could beat the rate. This suggests an incumbent's rate cut can pull the conversation away from declines unless we anchor it in what the failures cost.
competitor.quote: After the bank came back, every email was the rate.

message.finding: Lucy responded to the checkout and to Farah's explanation of why big-ticket orders get declined. Sam named nothing that got silence. Our proof of value was the generic average acceptance uplift slide, and it landed with the champion but not with the person deciding.
message.quote: When our solutions engineer, Farah, explained why big-ticket orders get knocked back and what we do about it, Lucy was nodding the whole way.

proof.finding: Lucy asked for a one-page business case she could hand Martin, and she got the deck and pricing proposal. Farah offered to put a dollar value on the failed orders from a three-month export, but it was never run because of end-of-quarter timing. In this deal, a customer-specific cost of the failing orders was the missing piece for the CFO.
proof.quote: Lucy asked once if we had something she could hand Martin. Like a one-page business case.

words.finding: Lucy described lost sales on big orders after all the work of winning the customer. We used the words declines, acceptance uplift and big-ticket orders. Her framing is about lost revenue on the biggest baskets, which is closer to the money argument the CFO needed than our rate-and-acceptance language.
words.quote: we do all the work to get someone to buy a four-thousand-dollar greenhouse and then the card says no.
